new_statements.quote: The Jukun Language is classified among the Nigritic languages (Shimuzu 1980, Ajiduku 2013). It is a “tone” language which uses pitch to indicate difference in the meaning of words. Most of the words in the Jukun language which are similar but have different tones will therefore, have different meanings (Ajiduku 13; 17)
new_statements.citation: Idris, Maryam Magaji Yusuf. 2021 [cited by others as Magaji 2017]. Linguistic variation: a problem for standardisation. A case study of the Jukuns of Taraba State. Ahyu: A Journal of Language and Literature (Federal University Wukari) 1: 70-78. doi:10.56666/ahyu.v1i.102
new_statements.locator: pp. 70-71 (Introduction); Wanu location list p. 71; 'the Wannu, Banu' p. 74; tone-marked Wanu wordlist tables pp. 74-77
new_statements.relation_note: States, for 'the Jukun Language' (explicitly including the Wanu variety compared in the paper), that it is a tone language in which pitch distinguishes word meanings; gives c. 40 tone-marked Wanu forms from the Ibadan 400 wordlist (pp. 74-77: Làpé 'water', Shíngyà 'urine', Abyíu 'oil', Āsà 'blood', Āfyù 'rain'..). Nothing on stress or accent; no count of tone levels.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Jukun (all varieties, Wanu included by the author) is lexically tonal; pitch differences distinguish otherwise identical words.
new_statements.identity_note: Compares four 'varieties of the Jukun language - Wapan, Ichen, Wanu and Kpanzo'; p. 71 'Wanu: Mainly in Abise, Ibi, Makurdi, Tella, Gindin Dorowa, Mayorenewo, Gbajimba, along the River Benue', p. 74 'the Wannu, "Banu"' = Wannu / Abinsi / River Jukun [jub] (Joshua Project 'Waanu ~ Baanu'). The tone statement itself is made of 'the Jukun Language' as a whole, on the authority of Ajiduku 2013 (a Wapan grammar), with Wanu treated as one of its dialects; it is not a Wanu-specific analysis.

Gives Wannu the vowel inventory /i ɪ e ɛ a ɑ ɔ o ʊ u/, the only language of 247 with that 10-vowel system (figure p. 387 'e.g., Wannu'; Appendix A p. 404, count 1). sources.citation: Meek, Charles Kingsley. 1931. A Sudanese Kingdom: an ethnographical study of the Jukun-speaking peoples of Nigeria. London: Kegan Paul, Trench, Trubner. xxxiii+548 pp.
sources.note: Ch. I (pp. 3-15) discusses only Wukari Jukun (= Wapan): p. 14 'In the Wukari dialect tones are significant, i.e. homonyms are distinguished by differences in tone'; no stress/accent statement anywhere (scanned a full-text search for stress/accent: 'stress'/'accent' only in non-linguistic senses). Abinsi (= Wannu) appears only as wordlist 'II Abinsi Dialect' in the Appendix from p. 505, with no prosodic commentary. Silent on stress for Wannu.

sources.citation: The Word for the World Nigeria & The Word for the World International. n.d. [2020s]. Afā Wanyɛnyɛ wu Nugé Wàpyóò (WBTP): the Gospel of Matthew (Mattuw) in Wannu. Digital scripture text, YouVersion version 4533; find.bible record JUBWFW.
sources.note: No descriptive content. The practical orthography marks tone with acute, grave and macron diacritics (plus unmarked vowels) on most words of running text (Mt 5:3 'Avosɔ̀ Shidɔ yi wu áwándó wàyì'wanɔ̀ la, wa nyànì nidi lá..'), i.e. tone-marked primary text implying a worked-out tone analysis by the translation team; this is data of the 'wordlist-only' kind, not a statement, and no orthography statement or phonology sketch from the project is online.
